key_terms.meaning: Dividing a curved surface into a grid of small flat polygons so it can be drawn; more triangles means a smoother shape and more cost.
A shape stored as a list of vertices plus a list of triangles, where each triangle names three vertex numbers instead of repeating their coordinates.
A unit vector stored at each vertex saying which way the surface points there; used to compute lighting without faceting.
A pair (u, v) given to each vertex that says which point of a 2D image (the texture) sticks to that vertex.
A 2D image pasted over a surface so a few polygons can show fine detail such as brick, wood or fabric.
The base colour a surface shows under even white light, before any shine or reflection is added.
A number, usually 0 to 1, saying how blurry or sharp the highlight on a surface is; 0 is mirror-like, 1 is matte.
A shape stored as a large set of 3D points with no triangles joining them, usually from a 3D scanner.
A shape defined by a formula f(x, y, z) = 0, so a point is on the surface when the formula gives zero.
A 4×4 array of numbers that moves, rotates or scales a point when the point's coordinates are multiplied by it.
A parent-child tree of objects where each child's transform is applied after its parent's, so moving the parent moves the whole group.
A simple box or sphere that fully contains an object, used for fast overlap tests before exact checks.
Finding whether and where two objects overlap, done in a cheap broad phase and an exact narrow phase.
Rules stored with an object that decide how it reacts to events such as a collision, a click or a timer.
Dividing x, y and z by w after projection, which is what makes far objects look smaller.
Turning each projected triangle into the list of screen pixels it covers, then shading those pixels.
Swapping an object for a simpler version when it is far away, keeping the triangle count inside the frame budget.
Skipping drawing any object whose bounding volume lies fully outside the camera's view pyramid.
Time from a real head movement to the pixel that shows the matching view changing on the display, in milliseconds.
A set of four numbers (w, x, y, z) with w² + x² + y² + z² = 1 that stores a 3D rotation without gimbal lock.

takeaways: A virtual object is geometry plus appearance, and both must be stored before the object can be placed or drawn.
An indexed mesh with vertex normals and UV coordinates is the usual way to store a textured, lit surface compactly.
Every world transform is a chain of matrix products running down the parent-child hierarchy from root to object.
Physics modelling has two jobs: detect contact cheaply with bounding volumes, then compute forces that change motion or surface shape.
Behaviour rules turn a static scene into a reactive one, and model management keeps that growing scene searchable.
The graphics pipeline runs in a fixed order: model, view, projection, clipping, perspective divide, viewport, rasterisation and fragment shading.
Real-time VR stays inside the frame budget by drawing only what is visible (culling) and only at the detail needed (LOD).
VR needs parallel hardware close to the eye, because a missed frame is felt as sickness, not just as a slow picture.
Yaw, pitch and roll are readable but suffer gimbal lock; unit quaternions avoid it and interpolate smoothly.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to move from definition to a worked transform or pipeline diagram and then to a justified design choice, so keep the matrix order, stage order and cost trade-offs explicit.

bank.q: A virtual object needs both geometry and visual appearance. Explain what each part contributes, and describe how an indexed mesh with vertex normals and UV coordinates stores a textured surface.
outline: Geometry = shape: vertices, edges, faces, stored as an indexed vertex list plus triangle list
Appearance = surface description: diffuse colour, roughness, specular level, textures
Vertex normals give per-pixel lighting so a low-polygon surface still looks smooth
UV coordinates map each vertex to a texture pixel; texture supplies detail without extra triangles
Tessellation trades triangle count for smoothness of curved surfaces

bank.q: Define tessellation, level of detail and texture. Explain why the tessellation level is a trade-off rather than a fixed setting.
outline: Tessellation: splitting a surface into small polygons
LOD: choosing a simpler version of the model with distance or screen size
Texture: 2D image mapped over the surface
More triangles improve silhouette and shading but cost vertex work and memory
VR must hold the frame budget, so detail is chosen per object per frame

bank.q: Explain how a parent-child object hierarchy produces world transforms. Write the chain of matrix products for a hand attached to a forearm attached to an upper arm attached to the body.
outline: Each object stores one local transform relative to its parent
World matrix = parent world × own local matrix
Chain: body × upper arm × forearm × hand
Order matters; matrix multiplication is not commutative
Moving a parent moves all children with no extra work; useful for avatars and machines

bank.q: List the stages of the graphics pipeline in order and state what each stage takes in and gives out.
outline: Model transform: object coordinates to world coordinates
View transform: world to camera coordinates
Projection: camera to clip coordinates, then clipping against the view volume
Perspective divide gives normalised device coordinates
Viewport transform maps to pixel coordinates
Rasterisation produces fragments; fragment shading computes colour; depth test resolves visibility

bank.q: Define motion-to-photon latency and frame budget. State the target values used in VR and explain why VR is stricter than desktop graphics.
outline: Frame budget = 1000 / refresh rate milliseconds; 90 Hz gives about 11 ms
Latency = time from head motion to the matching photons leaving the display
Targets are typically under about 20 ms total latency
Missed frames cause judder and simulator sickness because the view lags the head
Stereo doubles the work per frame

bank.q: A 2 m cube is centred at the local origin. Its parent rotates it 90° about the Y axis and then translates it 5 m along the world X axis. Give the 4×4 world matrix and compute the world coordinates of the local corner (1, 1, 1).
outline: Write rotation matrix R_y(90°) and translation T(5, 0, 0)
World matrix M = T × R; translation is applied last in world space
Multiply M by the homogeneous column (1, 1, 1, 1)
R_y(90°) sends (x, z) to (z, −x); corner becomes (1, 1, −1)
Add translation: world point = (6, 1, −1)
Check with a diagram and state units in metres

bank.q: A VR scene contains a temple model of 500,000 triangles. Apply level of detail: build three LOD levels and show how the triangle count per frame drops when 20 such models are visible at different distances.
outline: Example LOD chain: LOD0 500k, LOD1 100k, LOD2 20k, LOD3 a billboard of 2 triangles
Switch thresholds by screen-space size or distance, not by fixed metres alone
Sum the triangles for a stated mix of distances and compare against the budget
Mention hysteresis or blending to avoid visible popping
Also state that a large saving comes before LOD, from culling

bank.q: A point sits at camera coordinates (0, 0, −10) and the projection has vertical field of view 90°, aspect ratio 1, near 0.1 and far 100. Describe the projection step, the perspective divide and the final viewport mapping for a 2000×2000 pixel display.
outline: Build the projection matrix from fov, aspect, near, far
Multiply to get clip coordinates with w = 10 (for this symmetric case w = −z)
Perspective divide gives normalised device coordinates in [−1, 1]
Viewport transform maps to pixels: x_pix = (x_ndc + 1)/2 × width
State that depth becomes non-linear and most precision sits near the near plane

bank.q: Design a two-phase collision pipeline for a VR workshop where a user's hand tool must hit moving parts. Explain what is computed in each phase and what happens when an overlap is confirmed.
outline: Broad phase: bounding spheres or AABBs, or a spatial grid, to reject most pairs cheaply
Narrow phase: triangle-triangle or point-in-mesh test on the surviving pairs only
Compute contact point, contact normal and penetration depth
Force from penetration: spring-damper F = kx − cv along the contact normal
Force smoothing so the haptic device does not buzz, then mapping to device output
Hand the contact to the behaviour model to trigger a reaction

bank.q: Convert a yaw-pitch-roll triple into a rotation matrix and then into a unit quaternion. Explain why a VR tracker sends quaternions and how two orientations are interpolated.
outline: Yaw about Y, pitch about X, roll about Z; matrix is the product R_y × R_x × R_z
Standard matrix-to-quaternion conversion with sign choice on w
Normalise to remove drift in the four numbers
Quaternions avoid gimbal lock and interpolate by spherical linear interpolation
Compose rotations by quaternion multiplication; inverse is the conjugate for unit quaternions

bank.q: Compare workstation-based, distributed and standalone architectures for a VR training system. Recommend one for 20 trainees in one room on a limited budget and justify the choice.
outline: Workstation-based: one powerful PC per headset, easiest to develop, highest cost per user
Distributed: several machines share scene graph and physics over a network, scales but adds sync latency
Standalone: phone-class system on chip, cheap and untethered, limited fill rate and thermal headroom
Compare on cost per seat, latency, scene complexity and maintenance
Recommendation with a stated trade-off, for example standalone headsets plus one server for shared state
Mention consistency problems such as who owns physics for a shared object

bank.q: A scene runs at 60 fps on a desktop but only 30 fps on a standalone headset with the same content. Diagnose the cause using draw calls, fill rate, culling and LOD, and propose concrete fixes.
outline: Split the frame time into CPU (draw calls, physics, scripting) and GPU (vertex, fill, bandwidth)
Stereo rendering doubles geometry and fill work
Check overdraw and transparent surfaces: fill rate is the usual mobile limit
Add frustum and occlusion culling, then LOD and texture size reduction
Batch or instance repeated objects to cut draw calls
Re-measure and confirm the frame time is under the budget, not just the average fps

bank.q: Discuss physical and behaviour modelling together. How does a collision force change an object's motion and its surface, and how does the behaviour rule decide what the user sees and feels?
outline: Collision gives contact point, normal and depth
Force computation updates velocity and position, or deforms the surface
Surface deformation changes the mesh and possibly its normals and appearance
Behaviour model receives the event and runs its rule: sound, colour change, score, break apart
Force smoothing and mapping to a haptic device so the feel is stable
Discuss the cost: physics substeps must fit in the frame budget

bank.q: Analyse gimbal lock. Show where it appears in a yaw-pitch-roll head tracker and argue why quaternions are used instead.
outline: Yaw, pitch, roll apply three rotations in a fixed order about three axes
When pitch reaches ±90°, the yaw and roll axes line up and one degree of freedom is lost
Small changes then cause large jumps; interpolation between two triples misbehaves
Unit quaternion stores the same orientation in four numbers with no singularity
Spherical linear interpolation gives constant-speed, shortest-path blends
Cost: four numbers plus one normalisation, well inside the frame budget

glossary.def: The shape of a virtual object, stored as vertices, edges and faces in a mesh or point set.
The surface description (colour, roughness, specular level, textures) that decides how light leaves the object.
A single point of a 3D model, usually stored with its position, normal and texture coordinates.
The straight line joining two vertices of a polygon.
A flat polygon, usually a triangle, bounded by edges and used as the drawing unit of a mesh.
A mesh stored as a vertex array plus a triangle array that refers to vertices by number, avoiding duplicate data.
A unit vector perpendicular to a surface at a point, used to compute lighting and to test which side faces the camera.
Attaching a 2D image to a surface by giving each vertex UV coordinates into that image.
Writing a 3D point as four numbers (x, y, z, w) so translation, rotation and perspective can all be done by matrix multiplication.
A transform made only of rotation and translation, which keeps all distances and angles unchanged.
A tree of nodes holding transforms, geometry and behaviour, where children inherit their parent's transform.
A simple enclosing shape such as a sphere or box used for fast rejection tests in culling and collision.
The cheap first stage of collision detection that uses bounding volumes or spatial grids to discard object pairs.
The exact second stage that tests the actual triangles of the surviving pairs and reports the contact point.
What the system does after a contact is found: change velocity, deform the surface, play a sound or trigger a rule.
A behaviour model written as a set of states plus the events that move an object from one state to another.
The truncated pyramid of space visible to a camera, bounded by the near plane, far plane and four side planes.
A large nearby object that hides objects behind it and can be used to skip drawing what it blocks.
The number of pixels a GPU can shade per second, the usual limit when many large or transparent surfaces overlap.
One instruction from the CPU to the GPU to draw a batch of geometry; too many of them make the CPU the bottleneck.
A rotation stored as one unit axis plus one angle turned about that axis.
The loss of one rotational degree of freedom when two axes of a three-angle rotation line up.
The time allowed for one frame, equal to 1000 divided by the refresh rate in hertz, so about 11 ms at 90 Hz.
A per-pixel store of the nearest depth so far, used to decide which fragment wins when surfaces overlap.
